newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia overnight falls to 6.00/10 pct vs 8.5.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia overnight falls to 6.00/10 pct vs 8.5.

text.p: The overnight interbank rate fell sharply in late afternoon trade after a sudden induction of liquidity by some large local and foreign banks, dealers said on Tuesday.
They said the overnight rate, which was at over eight percent for the last two weeks, fell to 6.00/10 percent. It closed at 8.5 percent on Monday.
The overnight opened at 8.10/20 and maintained that level until the last half hour of trading, when it fell sharply.
"I don't really know where the liquidity came from. It seems like some big boys (banks) were making offers," said a dealer with a local bank.

Most other dealers were also unsure. They said there was no maturity of any government or central bank deposits, the usual source of liquidity. "If there was a maturity, the term rates in the morning would have also dipped," one dealer said.
Some dealers said it was possible that a large overseas payment came into the market, like petroleum royalty.

One dealer said there was a 500 million ringgit maturity of a Bank Negara 91-day bill issue on Friday which was not being rolled over by the central bank. "But, this still does not explain what happened today," he said.
Earlier, other interbank rates were mostly unchanged, though the market remained short of funds for up to one-week tenor.
However, rates quoted for commercial banks and finance companies were once again split sharply, dealers said.
They said finance companies continued to bid up rates for medium-term borrowings, while the same rates for commercial banks fell slightly.
Finance companies are considered higher credit risk in Malaysia and have to pay a premium on their interbank borrowings.
One-week money was available at 7.70/90 percent and two-week at 7.60/80, both unchanged from Monday.
One-month money was at 7.25/30 percent against 7.30/35, three-month at 30/35 against 7.42 and six-month at 7.40/45 against 7.43.
Dealers said an almost complete halt to an inflow of overseas funds and heavy borrowing by Bank Negara at its last open-market intervention was keeping interest rates firm.
They said foreign investors, who had been parking funds here due to political problems in Indonesia and Thailand, were returning to those countries.

The central bank regularly intervenes in the market to keep a check on liquidity or set interest rates, either through open tenders or by siphoning off funds directly from principal dealers. Its last intervention was on August 23.
